#863. Why are some football shin pads so small?

Liverpool striker Lewis Koumas (second from left) sported low socks and small shinpads on his full Premier League debut at Anfield

Liverpool's Lewis Koumas made his full Premier League debut against Manchester City on Sunday.

While doing so, he sported some very low socks over what appeared to be a very small shin pad.

Last season, images of Burnley's Marcus Edwards went viral after the 27-year-old was seen wearing barely visible shin pads during a Premier League match against West Ham.

Two years ago, a picture of teenager Harry Howell celebrating with James Milner while they were Brighton team-mates also gained attention after fans noticed the visible difference in the size of their shin pads.

Howell's 'micro' pair were an obvious contrast to Milner's far more traditional-sized guards.

So what is behind the trend of extra-small shin guards, and why are they used instead of regular-sized pairs?

The simple answer is that players can choose what size shin pads they want to wear.

The International Football Association Board (Ifab), responsible for the laws of the game, say that shin pads are a mandatory piece of equipment players must wear while playing.

Be of an appropriate size to provide reasonable protection and be covered by the socks

And players are responsible for the size and suitability of their shin pads

The law does not define what an "appropriate" shin pad size is, but leave that decision to each individual player.

Shin pads provide vital protection for players to prevent serious injuries.

There has been a rising trend in younger footballers, as well as some big stars, wearing small shin pads during matches.

The reason for this could be for more comfort and to allow players to move around with greater ease.

Referees are only required to check that some form of shin guards are being worn, Ifab told BBC Sport.

Ifab said players - or the parents or guardians of youth players - must take responsibility for their own safety on the pitch.

While shin pad size is ultimately an individuals choice, any decisions around player safety would also be made in consultation with their club and medical staff.

Marcus Edwards last year was seen wearing very small shin pads for Burnley in the Premier League

Grassroots football teams have started to ban small shin pads for safety reasons.

There are concerns that small shin pads do not cover the shins properly, which can lead to an increased risk of injury - especially at non-elite level.

In August 2024, a football club banned small shin pads after a youth player suffered a double leg break.

Penistone Church player Alfie Collins broke his tibia and fibula in a tackle during a game. The teenager's shin pads, which were no bigger than a credit card, were similar to a size recently worn by some stars of the professional game.

Shin pads "play an important role in injury prevention as they are intended to protect the shin from injury", the Football Association said.

"'Micro' or 'mini' shin pads may therefore increase the risk of injury due to the smaller amount of shin covered compared to larger sized shin pads," they added.

#862. Chelsea’s Alonso identity still to form in a midfield that remains a problem

Roméo Lavia’s resurgence is not enough as injuries to other key players such as Moisés Caicedo are proving disruptive

Xabi Alonso played for Pep Guardiola at Bayern Munich and was a key figure for Spain when their midfield dominated international football between 2008 and 2012. He does not need to be educated about the importance of control, but there has been a clear distinction between his identity as a player and how his Chelsea side have played.

Chelsea’s average possession stands at 47.8% after nine league games. They have made the eighth-most passes in the Premier League and are at their most dangerous on the counterattack. Give them space and they will run riot, but Alonso is yet to see a complete performance and knows they need to improve in midfield.

It is a problem area. Reece James has been out with a knee injury since September and the engine room lacks consistency. Alonso has experimented with different partnerships but is yet to settle on his favoured lineup and will be forced into another change if Chelsea find themselves without Moisés Caicedo when they visit Sunderland on Sunday afternoon.

The Ecuadorian, who has already had a spell on the sidelines with a calf injury, has not trained fully after feeling discomfort this week. It is a complication for Alonso, who keeps having to deal with injuries to key players. The striker João Pedro is out with a thigh injury, the centre-back Maxence Lacroix is hamstrung and there will have to be further adjustment if Caicedo cannot prove his fitness before Chelsea face the league’s bottom side.

Jordan Henderson is the obvious replacement for Caicedo. Chelsea could require the former’s experience given Sunderland probably need to turn the game into a battle, although they will also need poise in possession and are likely to get it from Roméo Lavia, whose elegance would make him an ideal in Alonso’s system if only it could be guaranteed his body was not going to let him down again.

We have been here before with Lavia, who has had little luck since joining from Southampton three years ago. The Belgium international barely played during his first season at Chelsea and has had plenty of false dawns since. The potential is not in doubt; the uncertainty is whether Lavia can stay fit.

Chelsea have not given up on the 22-year-old. Lavia has the talent to reach the top, but is he durable enough? He had not completed a full 90 minutes for Chelsea before going the distance during the Carabao Cup shootout defeat at Liverpool 10 days ago. That speaks volumes and is the reason for the caution, even though Lavia managed another 90 minutes when he produced a dominant display next to Caicedo during Chelsea’s 2-0 win against Manchester United last weekend.

Alonso needs more. He said Lavia had made changes to his physical preparation this season. “There has been a change,” Alonso said, although he did not elaborate. There is no suggestion Lavia has lacked professionalism. He is sensible, driven and smart. The suspicion is that it is more about being efficient from a conditioning perspective. Get that element right and Chelsea will have a top midfielder.

“Every time that the midfield area works, the team works better,” Alonso said. “We saw that Rom is in a very good place. I think that for the last month he has been very consistent in his performances, and he has been very important for the team, because in the middle you need to have a brain not just for yourself but a brain for the team.

“He’s good with the ball, he’s giving balance, he’s connecting very well with the players around him, with through balls. We need to push him, to help to continue, that it’s not enough, that he can take the next step. It’s not rocket science to know once you have good midfielders the team normally looks better.”

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Alonso needs that conductor to complement Caicedo’s power and ability to put out fires. Chelsea’s manager had Granit Xhaka knitting everything together when Bayer Leverkusen won the Bundesliga in 2024. It was not a surprise when Alonso tried to sign the Sunderland midfielder this summer.

“We spoke a lot in that time in Leverkusen with Granit because he was a key part of that team,” Alonso said. “He glued many pieces together.”

Chelsea are looking for similar cohesion. Alonso is yet to place his trust in Valentín Barco, signed from Strasbourg in the summer. The midfield is incomplete after the £125m sale of Enzo Fernández to Manchester City. A move for Monaco’s Lamine Camara broke down on deadline day and Bournemouth refused to sell Alex Scott after receiving inquiries from Arsenal, Chelsea and Liverpool for the newly capped England midfielder.

The situation will be revisited in January. Chelsea, who also like Crystal Palace’s Adam Wharton, are thought to have the edge over Liverpool in the race to sign Scott. They need to give Alonso more options in midfield. Lavia’s resurgence is not enough. Injuries elsewhere are disrupting Alonso’s plans, preventing him from making Chelsea consistent.

#861. Were any current Man City players signed during charges period?

Manchester City captain Ruben Dias has made more than 250 club appearances since his arrival in 2020

No member of Manchester City's current squad was signed during the period in which an independent commission found the club guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations.

Those offences all came between 2009 and 2018. City have denied any wrongdoing and appealed against all of the charges against them.

The club's longest-serving first-team player who was purchased from another club is Portuguese centre-back and club captain Ruben Dias, who joined from Benfica in 2020.

Norway striker Erling Haaland is the next longest-serving arrival, joining from Borussia Dortmund in the summer of 2022.

Midfielder Phil Foden is the only player to have played for the club during the period in which they breached the league's financial rules, but was not a senior signing having come through the club's youth ranks.

Foden, 26, made his first-team debut in a Champions League match against Feyenoord in November 2017.

Like Foden, versatile midfielder Rico Lewis is also a product of the club's academy but did not make his senior debut until August 2022.

All of the club's other senior players were signed between 2023 and 2026.

#860. Who is close to a yellow card suspension in Champions League?

Arsenal forward Kai Havertz is among the players to have received two yellow cards in this season's Champions League

Players will receive a one-match ban should they receive four yellow cards before the semi-finals of the Champions League.

This rule runs from the start of the league phase until the end of the quarter-finals. After then, all yellow cards are wiped out and players cannot be suspended for multiple yellow cards.

Yellow cards that result in a red card during a match do not count towards a player's tally, as a separate suspension will be served.

The same rules apply for both the Europa League and the Conference League.

During the opening three rounds of the Champions League, 16 players received two yellow cards, meaning they are now two cautions away from a one-match ban.

Shakhtar Donetsk's Marlon Gomes, Villarreal's Santiago Mourino and Inter Milan's Hakan Calhanoglu are each on three yellow cards, putting them on the brink of a ban.

Players can also be suspended if they pick up six, eight or 10 yellow cards. This would also result in a one-match suspension every time a player hits an even number of yellow cards above four.

Red cards result in a one-match suspension, with Bayern Munich's Michael Olise missing his side's earlier clash with Arsenal after being sent off against Viking in the previous round of fixtures.

Uefa may increase the length of a red card ban for serious offences such as violent conduct.

*denotes two yellows that resulted in a red card

The following players will miss the next round of league phase matches following either a yellow or red card suspension:

Matheus Cunha (Manchester United - red card suspension)

#859. Serbian police shoot dead assailant at Israeli Embassy

A "minor" has been killed by police after attacking a guard at Israel's embassy in Belgrade with knives, the interior minister says. Ivica Dacic said police had declared the highest terror alert after the incident.

A knife-wielding assailant attacked a police guard outside the Israeli Embassy in the Serbian capital, Belgrade, overnight to Wednesday, slightly wounding the officer before being shot dead by him, Serbia's interior minister said.

Interior Minister Ivica Dacic said the attacker, whom he described as a minor, had been monitored by security agencies as a supporter of the terrorist organization "Islamic State" (IS).

Israel's Foreign Ministry later confirmed an "attempted terrorist attack" near its embassy in Belgrade, adding that no personnel were injured and the incident was being investigated.

The attacker was thought to come from the western Serbian town of Sabac and "kept the black flag in support of the 'Islamic State' on his Instagram” account," according to the minister.

Dacic said the assailant shouted "Allahu Akbar," or "God is great" in Arabic, during the attack on the guard. According to Dacic, the guard killed the attacker in self-defense.

He said police were treating the incident as a terrorist attack, with the terrorism threat level raised to its highest, or "red alert."

"This means tighter security checks and an increased police presence at sensitive sites, including infrastructure facilities and places where large crowds gather," he said.

The attack came  just days after key early parliamentary election in Serbia and one day after Israel held its parliamentary vote, with no clear result yet in sight.

In June 2024, an attacker with a crossbow seriously wounded a Serbian police officer guarding the same embassy in Belgrade before being shot and killed by police.

That attacker was identified as a 25-year-old Islamic convert from a village near the capital who had become radicalized.

#858. WNBA Stars Paige Bueckers, Azzi Fudd Confirm Breakup

Dallas Wings’ teammates Paige Bueckers and Azzi Fudd confirmed they broke up “over a year ago” in the WNBA rookie’s podcast Fudd Around and Find Out.

Paige Bueckers and Azzi Fudd pulled a pass fake on WNBA fans.

The Dallas Wings teammates—who confirmed their relationship in July 2025—shared they are no longer together, and haven’t been for over a year.

Welcoming Bueckers to the Nov. 6 episode of her Fudd Around and Find Out podcast, Fudd confirmed the news as the former couple laughed it off, quipping, “I don’t know how else to say that.”

Bueckers also confirmed that the duo—who first sparked romance rumors during their time playing basketball together at University of Connecticut—had been broken up for “over a year.”

In fact, it was well before they knew they would be stepping onto the court together.

“To share that now everybody’s gonna be like, ‘Oh my gosh they’re teammates. How is this going to work?’” Bueckers explained. “We were not together before she got drafted so all those narratives can go to bed. She was not drafted because she was my girlfriend. She was drafted because she deserved it.”

The 25-year-old emphasized that she and Fudd—who was drafted in April—remain friends.

“She’s an amazing human, an amazing basketball player,” she continued. “We’re still friends, we’re still cool. We broke up over a year ago, so we played an entire season together. We’re the utmost professional. We care about basketball.”

Bueckers also acknowledged that she wanted to give a “speech” regarding the fan’s obsession with their romance since it was confirmed.

“There’s a whole list and notes of things that I would love to address if I had the time or the energy but I think and Azzi can agree to this just to start by saying we don’t stand for hate of any kind,” the guard continued. “We don’t condone that. If you’re using our names and our image to spread that, that’s not who we are and that’s not what we’re about.”

Nodding to the negative messages Bueckers and Fudd’s family, friends and teammates received during their relationship, Bueckers acknowledged, “That’s never been something that we’ve stood for.”

Ultimately, both Bueckers and Fudd, 23, made it clear they only support each other—and only want support for each other from their fans.

“We’re still going to be great teammates,” Bueckers continued. “We’re going to be professionals. We are still going to have other friends. We will eventually move on.”

She also didn’t want any hate for their potential future partners joking, “I know we will continue to be outside and be lit and have a good time so we should not get punished for that as well.”

Fudd, for her part, concurred with everything Bueckers laid out, and confirmed they won’t be speaking any further on their relationship.

“We know you guys are probably curious and have a ton of questions,” she acknowledged, “but we’ve addressed everything that we need to and the rest will stay with us.”

For a deeper look into the love lives of WNBA stars, keep reading…

Still, there have been definitive clues that the Bayou Barbie has found her Ken in Orlando Magic center Wendell Carter Jr. "That’s a sign," the Atlanta Dream power forward captioned a TikTok showcasing an impressive arrangements of roses, "that’s a signnnn." And it was certainly a big play when the Duke alum turned up to the 2025 WNBA All-Star game sporting a t-shirt baring Reese's visage.

The NCAA champ—set to appear on season two of The Hunting Wives—returned the favor, attending a December 2025 Magic game in a jersey emblazoned with the words "My Man."

Game recognizes game, and three-time WNBA champion A'ja Wilson has found her ace of hearts in Bam Adebayo.

The low-key couple first sparked dating rumors in the summer of 2024, and Wilson confirmed their romance with a bit of a pump fake when she showed up at NBA All Star Weekend in February 2025.

"My NBA All-Star is not here," the Las Vegas Aces center told People, acknowledging that the Miami Heat center hadn't made the roster. But Adebayo was busy "getting the rest he needs," she added, "and that's the best Valentine gift that I can truly give him, is just the rest."

And they're only heating up, Adebayo showing up to support Wilson—who made her fifth straight All-Star team—during the WNBA All-Star festivities in July 2025.

Months later, in her TIME Athlete of the Year cover story, she revealed they'd actually been huddled up way longer than fans realized, making that first move at the Tokyo Olympics in 2021.

Next up: Adding to their squad. "That is always a dream," she said of having kids with Adebayo. "This is my life partner. Honestly, what on earth was my world before you? That’s how much he’s impacted my life, my family’s life."

Sabrina Ionescu has racked up an impressive haul of trophies playing for the New York Liberty, WNBA All-Stars and U.S. Olympic team, but the day she married NFL player Hroniss Grasu is especially close to her heart.

"March 10, 2024. The day I got to marry my best friend, my other half," she captioned her Instagram wedding photo. "The best day of my life."

Marta Xargay Casademont & Breanna Stewart

Three-time WNBA champion Breanna Stewart met her love match with Spanish basketball player Marta Xargay Casademont. They connected as teammates on a Russian professional women's basketball team in 2018 and got engaged and married in 2021. They welcomed their first child Ruby in August 2021, followed by their son Theo in October 2023.

Xargay Casademont retired from the sport in 2021, but continues to support her wife's career, writing on Instagram after Stewart's New York Liberty won the 2024 Finals, "So freaking proud of you!"

Indiana Fever megastar Caitlin Clark has been dating basketball player and former Butler University assistant coach Connor McCaffery since April 2023.

The pair haven't been shy about celebrating their love on social media, with McCaffery posting a sweet birthday tribute for his girlfriend's January 2025 birthday: "You have an incredible ability to inspire and lift up those around you, and I am lucky to learn from you every day. Thank you for always being you. I love you."

New York Liberty shooting guard and 2021 WNBA All-Star Betnijah Laney is married to fellow basketball player Jordan Hamilton, who started for the Denver Nuggets, New Orleans Pelicans, and Houston Rockets during his NBA career.

In an Instagram tribute for their second wedding anniversary in 2023, Laney wrote, "Your arms are my favorite place to be."

After dating for eight years, Diana Taurasi married her Phoenix Mercury teammate Penny Taylor on May 13, 2017. Now both retired from the sport, the iconic WNBA couple have more time to spend with their children, Leo and Isla.

After a few weeks of speculation, Dallas Wings point guard Paige Bueckers confirmed in July 2025 that she was dating Azzi Fudd, her former teammate on the UConn’s women’s basketball team.

And with Fudd selected first overall by the Wings in the 2026 draft, the two were thrilled to pair up on and off the hardwood. "I'm excited to play again with Paige," Fudd told ESPN during draft night April 13. "She's an incredible person. An incredible player, and it's gonna be a lot of fun."

In November 2026, though, the couple confirmed they had broken up "over a year" prior.

"We’re still friends, we’re still cool," Bueckers explained during an appearance on Fudd's Fudd Around and Find Out podcast. "We broke up over a year ago, so we played an entire season together. We’re the utmost professional. We care about basketball.”

Prior to playing for the Indiana Fever in 2024 and re-joining the Seattle Storm in February 2025, Katie Lou Samuelson was busy with her life off the court. She married basketball player Devin Cannady in April 2023 and the couple announced the birth of their daugher Aliya in August 2023.

WNBA superstar Napheesa Collier can add devoted wife and mom to her long list of achievements (which includes two Olympic gold medals and 2025 All-Star Game MVP).

In October 2019, the Minnesota Lynx forward got engaged to basketball skills coach Alex Bazzell and they were married three years later. In 2022, they welcomed daughter Mila Sarah Bazzell.

Then-Chicago Sky teammates Allie Quigley and Courtney Vandersloot were married in December 2018 and share daughter Jana, who was born on April 8, 2025.

The winning pair are not only the first married couple to win a professional sports championship together (the 2021 WNBA Finals), but in May 2025, a month before Quigley announced her retirement, Vandersloot surpassed her wife's record as the all-time leading scorer for the Chicago Sky.

In March 2021, Alyssa Thomas shared on social media that she was dating her then-Connecticut Sun teammate, DeWanna Bonner.

The pair got engaged in 2023 when Thomas proposed during the WNBA All-Star Weekend. Bonner is also mom to Cali and Demi, the twins she welcomed in 2017 with ex-wife and former Phoenix Mercury teammate Candice Dupree.

#857. Rise of the ‘schooligans’: how a wave of antisocial behaviour threatens non-league football

Teenage ultras are increasingly causing disorder and communities fear it will not be long before it becomes something more dangerous

It is five past three on Saturday afternoon and the teenage ultras of Hednesford Town are running late. They have arrived in Chester for their team’s National League North fixture and have hailed taxis, determined to make their presence felt at the ground. But word appears to have got out about their arrival. As one car turns away from the city’s charming half-timbered houses and into narrow residential streets, half a dozen local youths appear, haring round the corner in balaclavas. They try to attack the cab and chase after it as it pulls away. The smell of pyro is everywhere. As the taxi finally gets clear, the Chester gang stops in the middle of the road, shouting and gesticulating. One lad, no older than 16, pulls a long blade from inside his trousers and brandishes it.

The incident ended there and no one was hurt, though a police investigation has been launched. The match went off without trouble too and the Hednesford gang – known at home as the “schooligans” – were escorted safely back to the station by Cheshire police. It was just another weekend in English non-league football, where a wave of antisocial behaviour is causing concern and leading the UK Football Policing Unit (UKFPU) to declare it its “most important” priority. As the disorder continues, a question remains: how long will it be before teenage trouble-making becomes something more dangerous?

This year clubs from the south coast to the north-east have reported disorder caused by supporters under the age of 18, some seemingly as young as 10. In February, Aldershot Town experienced a series of disorderly incidents involving young people that included brawls outside the ground, behaviour the club described as “wholly unacceptable and [which] will not be tolerated”. In August, Enfield Town said they were “concerned and disappointed” by young fans at a fixture in Lewes. Two weeks ago, a Gloucester City fan was hit by a rock thrown by teenagers at Redditch United during an FA Trophy tie. Even Soham Town Rangers of the ninth-tier Eastern Counties League urged parents to ensure their children make “sensible choices” ahead of a match against Mildenhall Town.

Hednesford have experienced consistent trouble for a number of seasons and in August their owner and chair, Craig Gwilt, attempted to face it down. A rising tide of disorder was harming the club, he said, behaviour that included “pitch invasions, fighting, abuse directed towards players, missiles being thrown at opposition goalkeepers, flares entering the field of play and even interference with players’ water bottles”. He called on fans to improve their behaviour or risk permanently damaging the club. The plea was not immediately heard. Three weeks after Gwilt’s statement the club banned 20 young supporters from attending matches after there was action away at Telford.

Hednesford is a town of 19,000 people on the edge of the protected landscape of Cannock Chase. The town centre is neat and tidy, a well-maintained monument to the Stafford regiment at its heart. On the way to the ground you can get a pint at the Cross Keys where Dick Turpin reputedly rested his head. It’s a town seemingly at peace with itself and the club is at the heart of the community. But both are struggling to get to grips with an issue that leaves people scratching their heads.

This season the club have introduced measures to prevent under-16s from entering without an accompanying adult. There is also extra security on matchdays, ostensibly to manage car parking. These interventions appear to have contained any trouble in and around the stadium, but now gangs of up to 50 youths will gather post-match at a safe remove to look for trouble or, more likely, save their energy for an away fixture. Like the one at Chester, for example, when the schooligans were removed from one train for antisocial behaviour and were drinking alcohol throughout their journey up. Encountering such groups on a Saturday will be familiar to many rail passengers.

The schooligans, whose nickname was coined by Hednesford’s security staff, “baffle” the club’s chief executive, Marvin Robinson, who would rather be spending his time modernising a club that have had back-to-back promotions. “I’m not really sure I understand why it seems to be a trend,” he says. “It’s a wider social issue but what is it and what will it become? Is it a social media thing? Is it about notoriety or becoming known for something? The adult response online has been almost to normalise it. I don’t agree with that.”

Go on TikTok and the picture does start to become a little clearer. From aggregator accounts to individual semi-anonymised accounts belonging to the teenagers, there is a wealth of posts celebrating the behaviour of “top lads” who “mooch” to the ground before “running” the opposition out of town. Often set to a backing of euphoric electronic dance music with a layer or two of visual effects and captions such as “this weekend’s got me feeling like a little kid at Christmas”, the posts are celebratory and almost nostalgic in tone. In recent weeks TikTok has begun appending disclaimers to them that read: “Participating in this activity could result in you or others getting hurt.” TikTok removed an account named “NLN [National League North] gimps and chants”, when alerted to it by the Guardian, for contravening guidelines that do not allow content that glorifies violence.

The mythology of old-school football hooliganism appears to be well‑known among these groups, with references to the 2005 film Green Street commonplace. But the schooligans of 2026 don’t behave like the firms of the past. For a start they rarely, if at all, arrange to fight their rivals. Instead they use the mapping feature on Snapchat to alert opposition to their presence on the day, and take it from there. The concept of rivalry itself is fluid. In the West Midlands, for example, teens from Hednesford will band together with those nominally affiliated with Redditch or Cannock Town. When there was trouble recently at Hednesford’s fixture at Hereford, local police said the majority of disorder had been caused by Redditch fans chasing supporters from Solihull Moors. It isn’t just local either. Children as young as 12 have been detained in the north-west having travelled from the south coast, a distance of more than 200 miles.

The chair of Redditch, David Faulkner, is still dealing with the fallout from the Gloucester tie two weeks ago. He says the fluid set of alliances between ultra groups has created a “travelling circus” and that no one knows where it will turn up next. Branding himself “the non-League chair”, Faulkner has started posting videos on YouTube drawing attention to the disorder and calling for collective action.

“People think of non-league football as one man and his dog, but we need to catch up with the fact that it’s massive now,” Faulkner says. “Some clubs have attendances bigger than in League One but the regulations were put in place decades ago. We need that extra regulation, that support, so we can get the funding to put things like CCTV and more stewarding in place. Because the other way this could go is that [change only happens] when someone gets seriously hurt. I haven’t got metal detectors on our gates to stop kids bringing knives in. None of that stuff. I’d rather take action before something happens.”

The Football Association says the behaviour of fans is primarily a matter for clubs and relevant authorities but that it is working to develop policies that welcome young fans safely to National League grounds. The UK Football Policing Unit, meanwhile, is working alongside leagues and the Crown Prosecution Service to develop new policies around “youth risk”, which are likely to include an extra focus on education via schools and community work.

“It’s probably the most important area of football policing that we’re focused on,” says Mike Ankers, the deputy director of the UKFPU. “We are seeing children as young as 12 or 13 engaged in antisocial behaviour at best, but also actual violence and that’s up and down the country, with some travelling hundreds of miles. There comes a great risk and a great safeguarding issue with regards to that. In terms of our focus, we are making sure that we bring the right people together to have a solution. It’s not just the policing, it requires a more holistic view.”

Ankers says he supports Faulkner in speaking up on the topic and believes many more adults need to take responsibility. “These children need a strong adult role model,” he says. “I would very much question that if your 12-year-old is going out to follow football and is being detained, perhaps 200 miles away, then you need to look at how they’ve been able to travel and have those conversations. I think there’s very much a role for parental responsibility.”

The Hednesford schooligans, having been deposited on the platform at Chester by police, made their way home by train, only to find themselves stuck in a combination of Halloween revellers and national signal failure. Constrained, they hunched over their phones viewing footage from different teenage firms and discussed the day’s events. In the end, they concurred they had got the best of it. After all, said one: “What experience do you get from chasing a taxi?”

TikTok and Snapchat were approached for comment.

#856. Which game will Chelsea's Palmer miss after red card?

Cole Palmer was sent off in the second half of Chelsea's 2-0 loss at Stamford Bridge

Chelsea's Cole Palmer will not miss the Blues' Premier League meeting with Manchester United on Saturday, despite being sent off in his side's last Premier League match.

Palmer was shown two yellow cards in the second half of the Blues' defeat by rivals Tottenham Hotspur on Saturday. That dismissal meant that Palmer was handed a one-match ban.

The England playmaker was shown his first caution for an off-the-ball incident involving Spurs' Mateus Fernandes. He was then shown a second yellow card for a foul on Conor Gallagher.

In most cases, this would be served in that team's next Premier League match. However, Palmer will not miss Chelsea's meeting with United at Stamford Bridge.

Instead, Palmer will be banned for the Blues' EFL Cup fourth-round match away at Liverpool on Wednesday night.

This is because red card suspensions are carried out across domestic competitions rather than being specific to the competition they were received in.

Suspensions for an accumulation of yellow cards across a campaign are served in the competition in which they are received.

So while the Blues will miss Palmer for their trip to Anfield, he will be available to face United three days after the club's cup tie on Merseyside.

#855. Which Premier League players are set for yellow card suspensions?

Matty Cash and Matt Crooks are the first players of the 2025-26 Premier League season to pick up a yellow card suspension

Hull City's Matt Crooks and Aston Villa's Matty Cash have become the first players to receive a one-match ban for accumulating five yellow cards in the 2025-26 Premier League season.

Crooks will be suspended for Hull's trip to Arsenal after receiving a yellow card against Ipswich at the weekend, while Cash will miss Villa's match at Manchester United after being booked for a foul against Fulham.

Players receive a one-match suspension if they pick up five or more yellow cards prior to the conclusion of their team's 19th league match of the season.

Six other players are sitting on four bookings after nine rounds of matches, meaning they must avoid another yellow card prior to the halfway point of the season to avoid a ban.

After that date, the threshold increases to 10 yellow cards. Any player reaching that number before the end of their club's 32nd league match of the season will receive a two-match suspension.

From that point, there are further thresholds at 15 and 20 yellow cards.

For players reaching 15 cautions, they incur a three-match suspension. Punishments for players reaching 20 yellow cards are determined by a regulatory commission.

Those cut-offs do not reset until the end of the Premier League season.

In the Championship, League One and League Two, there are similar thresholds.

However, with those three divisions having 46 rounds of league matches instead of 38, players have to avoid getting 10 yellow cards before the end of the 37th league match in order to not receive a two-match suspension.

In those divisions, the yellow cards are reset at the end of the league season and do not include matches in the play-offs.

If any of the following players receive another Premier League yellow card before the season's halfway point, they will be banned for one match:

Pascal Gross - Brighton & Hove Albion (four)

The following players will miss their club's next set of fixtures:

Matt Crooks - Hull City (yellow card suspension)

Matty Cash - Aston Villa (yellow card suspension)

Max Dowman - Arsenal (red card suspension)

Jean-Philippe Mateta - Crystal Palace (red card suspension)

Lisandro Martinez - Manchester United (red card suspension)

Omar Alderete - Sunderland (red card suspension)

#853. Amar Dedic set to escape Newcastle sanction over carrying bow and arrow

Right-back sparked armed police response over incident

Expected to start Newcastle’s trip to Fulham on Saturday

Newcastle’s Amar Dedic is unlikely to face a club sanction after being spotted holding a bow and arrow in the Northumberland countryside and sparking a major police pursuit involving an armed response unit.

Dedic is expected to start Newcastle’s match at Fulham on Saturday after an incident that at one point saw six patrol cars pursue the ­Bosnia right‑back back to his home on the Darras Hall estate, just ­outside Ponteland.

Northumbria police were alerted on Wednesday afternoon when a member of the public spotted Dedic and a friend walking through the Northumberland countryside equipped with bows and arrows. This equipment was eventually seized from the boot of the 24-year-old’s car when he arrived back home at Darras Hall.

In a statement the force said they were satisfied the bows and arrows were “for recreational use and there was no threat to the public”, but inquiries were “ongoing”. Pursuing animals using bow and arrows or crossbows is illegal in the UK but there are no suggestions that Dedic or his friend were on a hunting expedition.

“Shortly after 1.55pm on Wednesday we received a report of two men carrying a bow and arrow while walking along a track by the reservoir on the Military Road in the Harlow Hill area,” said Northumbria police. “Officers attended and subsequently stopped a vehicle in the Darras Hall area and seized bows and arrows.”

Dedic, a £29.5m summer signing from Benfica, is believed to have been grateful for the coincidental intervention of Newcastle’s fourth-choice goalkeeer Mark Gillespie and former full-back Paul Dummett. The pair were passing Dedic’s home and, spotting the police presence on his driveway, stopped to offer assistance and are understood to have helped calm the situation down. Newcastle are understood to believe Dedic acted “naively”.

#851. Bellinghams celebrate ‘beautiful story’ as Jobe joins Jude in Tuchel’s England 2.0

Jude had asked head coach to scout Dortmund midfielder

‘It will be beautiful for Jude to have his brother close’

Thomas Tuchel has given a first England call-up to Jobe Bellingham, admitting the midfielder’s older brother, Jude, had nagged him to do so, as he set up the prospect of their family dream being realised.

Tuchel’s inclusion of the younger Bellingham for the Nations League games against Croatia and Spain was further evidence of his shift away from the squad that served him well at the World Cup last summer and towards a fresh dynamic for the mission to win Euro 2028. The manager has named a 25-man group for the game against Croatia at Wembley on Thursday and the one against Spain in Madrid three days after; of the 22 outfield players, only 11 were at the World Cup.

Jobe Bellingham, the England Under-21s captain, has impressed for Borussia Dortmund this season and Jude is on record as saying how much it would mean if they could play together for their country, especially at a major tournament. “It would be the biggest dream of my life,” he said. “It would mean more than any of the trophies I have won.”

Tuchel said the brothers coming together in his England squad was a “beautiful story” and he wondered whether Jobe’s presence could inspire Jude to even greater heights. “Let’s see what the effect is,” Tuchel said. “Jude always behaves like a big brother, taking care of his younger brother. I think that helps Jobe now in camp. And it will be beautiful for Jude to have his brother close.

“Me and Jude spoke about his brother because I was aware it was always his dream [to play for England with Jobe]. Jude was always like: ‘Watch him, watch him, he’s good, he can make it.’ I would say: ‘Yeah, we are watching him.’ And we know, of course, [about him] from Lee Carsley [the under-21s manager].”

Tuchel described Jobe as “maybe more a No 8 than a classic 6 and less of a 10”. He noted that with Myles Lewis-Skelly suspended against Croatia, Jobe’s chances of being involved were higher. It has been 19 years since Gary and Phil Neville were the last brothers to play together for England.

Tuchel accidentally referred to Jobe as “Jube” at one point, a slip that will doubtless be made by others, and said it was a special moment to break the news of the call-up to him on a video call. “He couldn’t stop smiling,” Tuchel said. “He has the same beautiful smile as Jude.”

It is clear that Tuchel’s relationship with Jude Bellingham is on a secure footing, as opposed to this time last year when the player’s place in the squad was in doubt – and certainly his spot in the XI. “It was a bit of an up and down [relationship] but we are in a good place,” Tuchel said. “I hope we have finished with the down. You never know as a coach!”

Goalkeepers Jordan Pickford (Everton), Jason Steele (Brighton), James Trafford (Leeds United)

Defenders Trent Alexander-Arnold (Real Madrid), Jarrad Branthwaite (Everton), Marc Guéhi (Manchester City), Lewis Hall (Newcastle United), Ezri Konsa (Arsenal), Jarell Quansah (Bayer Leverkusen), Djed Spence (Inter), Ben White (Arsenal)

Midfielders Elliot Anderson (Manchester City), Jobe Bellingham (Borussia Dortmund), Jude Bellingham (Real Madrid), James Garner (Everton), Josh King (Fulham), Myles Lewis-Skelly (Arsenal), Declan Rice (Arsenal)

Forwards Dominic Calvert-Lewin (Leeds United), Eberechi Eze (Arsenal), Morgan Gibbs-White (Nottingham Forest), Anthony Gordon (Barcelona), Harry Kane (Bayern Munich), Rio Ngumoha (Liverpool), Morgan Rogers (Chelsea)

More broadly, Tuchel looked reinvigorated after the success of the September/October camp when his team won three out of four Nations League ties to all but guarantee a place in the quarter-finals. Tuchel had been tense at the start of the get-together as he was assailed by the fallout from the World Cup semi-final defeat by Argentina.

He made some ruthless decisions in September, discarding Noni Madueke, Ollie Watkins and Ivan Toney from the squad he took to the World Cup. Dean Henderson, Dan Burn and Jordan Henderson, picked in the summer and fit again, have been left out, while Kobbie Mainoo and Nico O’Reilly, who is a managing an injury, were also not selected. He overlooked Cole Palmer and Phil Foden. Missing through injury are Reece James, Tino Livramento, John Stones, Trevoh Chalobah, Alex Scott, Bukayo Saka and Marcus Rashford.

Tuchel has placed an emphasis on youth in his post-World Cup selections and he added Josh King to the squad on Friday. The 19-year-old attacking midfielder’s only previous involvement was at the pre-World Cup training camp in Florida. Tuchel has also given a recall to the more experienced right-back Ben White.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

It was put to Tuchel that his squad had the look of an England 2.0. “It has to be like this,” he said. “We said at some point that we need to take the next step, otherwise you’re left behind. You need to bring in new players for competition; young players, fresh energy. I was a bit worried in the last camp because we were missing so many internal leaders but the group did excellently in a new style, in a new leadership way but in their style. Now there’s a little bit of proof of concept. We give the players the opportunity and responsibility.”

Tuchel namechecked his current leaders as Harry Kane, Saka, Jude Bellingham, Elliot Anderson, Declan Rice, Ezri Konsa and Marc Guéhi. He said he had spoken to them on day one of the last camp – although not Rice, because he had withdrawn – about the need for them “to make sure we have the same standards as at the World Cup”.

Were the seven players the leadership group? “Per se,” Tuchel replied. “I said straight away that I want to have a group that starts matches regularly. These were the players – without having a guarantee. But I said: ‘I want you to start these matches and you make sure that the energy, attitude, the standards within the group are at the highest level.’ That has not changed. So they are basically a leadership group on the field.”

Tuchel said Palmer’s exclusion was “not personal … but the competition is on. It’s about the ones who walk the walk and come to camp”. He made it sound as if Foden was closer to a recall.

“Phil is always an option because I’m in love with him as a player,” Tuchel said. “It was very close. It’s also close for Eberechi Eze to keep his place with us. He’s not starting for Arsenal. The advantage was maybe that Eberechi and Morgan Gibbs-White were in camp last time. They need to fight for it. That’s what we want. And Phil is always close.”

Tuchel also commented on Mainoo’s omission. He took the midfielder to the World Cup but did not play him. “He was hugely disappointed from the World Cup and deservedly so,” Tuchel said. “I said in front of the team and the staff: ‘Sorry, I didn’t pick you. You did nothing wrong. That is on me.’ I think it cost him a bit of confidence. Then he pulled out of the last camp when I was desperate to include him in this new start. And then he entered a difficult spell. He was injured and Man United fell off a cliff a little bit performance-wise.”

#849. Hailee Steinfeld Reveals What She Didn’t Expect From Motherhood

Hailee Steinfeld detailed what she’s learned about herself from the “transformative experience” of being a mom to her and Josh Allen’s baby girl Harper.

Hailee Steinfeld is learning to play new notes as a first-time mom.

Six months after she gave birth to baby girl Harper with husband Josh Allen, the Pitch Perfect 2 star shed light on the unexpected impact motherhood has had on her relationship with herself.

“There’s a long answer, but I’ll give the short one here: I’ve learned just how much of myself I still have to discover,” Steinfeld wrote the Nov. 3 edition of her Beau Society newsletter on Substack, in response to a fan question. “I thought becoming a mom would be this transformative experience about loving someone else, and it is that 1000 percent.”

“But what I didn’t expect is how much she’s teaching me about myself,” she added. “She’s made me more patient, more present, and so much more aware of how special the little things are.”

And as the Hexed actress continues to discover new aspects about herself amid her motherhood journey, she’s also learning to take her own advice.

“I’m really good at reminding people that they’re human, that things take time, and that everything happens for a reason,” Steinfeld wrote, “and it will all fall into place—how, when, and where it should—and that they don’t have to have everything all figured out.”

Yet, she admitted, “I’m not always the best at taking that advice myself.”

But since becoming a mom, the Sinners star—who married Allen in May 2025—has made sure that her own wellbeing is still a priority.

“This season of life has definitely taught me to slow down, really just soak in the small pockets of joy that are truly all around us,” she shared on the Nov. 5 episode of Live With Kelly and Mark. “Time for myself looks a little different now, but I find it.”

And this mindset of cherishing every moment is surely beneficial when it comes to wrapping her heard around how fast her daughter is growing up.

“I feel like she’s 6 months, and also 4 weeks, and also 5 years old,” Steinfeld told Kelly Ripa and Mark Consuelos. “Time is crazy how it works.”

“She is totally on the move,” she added. “This girl is crawling around.”

#848. Africa's first Youth Olympics open in Senegal amid hope and scrutiny

Senegal is hosting Africa's first Youth Olympics, with 2,700 young athletes competing in Dakar, Diamniadio and Saly. The Games bring pride and hope, but also questions over cost, rights and legacy.

On the final day of October, what may well be the final Summer Youth Olympics ever will begin. It will be the first on African soil as around 2,700 athletes aged 15-17 arrive in Senegal to compete across a total of 153 events in 25 sports.

Hosted in eight venues across three locations – Dakar, Diamniadio and Saly, 80 kilometers (50 miles) from the capital – these Games are seen by many as a prelude to Africa hosting a full Olympics one day in the future.

"I'm really excited about the Youth Olympic Games because, for the first time, I'll be representing our country," 15-year-old judoka Aisha Diop who is competing for Senegal told DW.

"I am very proud to be able to represent my country at these Games. This will really motivate young African athletes because they will improve, and they will want to continue playing sports now that the Youth Games have been held here."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The 2026 Youth Games in Senegal will also be a first beyond the history it is making in Africa.

"Of the 2,700 athletes who will be competing in Dakar, there will be a 50-50 split between men and women," Olivia Nloga, Chief Brand Promotion Officer on the organizing committee, told DW.

"But this parity isn't just reflected in the overall figure. This gender parity will also be reflected in each event and in each sport where such parity actually exists."

Several sports are also making their debut at the Youth Olympic Games, such as five-a-side baseball, kung fu and the Senegalese specialty of beach wrestling. There's also a refugee team at the Youth Olympic Games for the first time.

"As I said earlier, the Youth Olympic Games aren't just about sports, and they aren't just about infrastructure," said Nloga.

"For us, it was also important to use this time to build on and reinforce the idea that these Games in Senegal are a celebration for the people. We did this by investing in culture—for example, through a fashion show and a program called Yi-sol, which is a mural project on the city's walls."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Other projects designed to celebrate the people include music, and a local student designed the mascot. The biggest focus of all though, is on creating sustainability for the young people of Senegal.

"We did so through a program that is very important to us – one that is close to our hearts, namely, the Olympic Civic and Sports Certificate," Nloga said.

"We traveled to schools throughout Senegal and worked with more than 1,000 instructors to reach and make an impact on more than one million young Senegalese children who, during this hiatus, were exposed to and educated about the values of the Olympic Movement."

With recent flooding in the country, there were concerns that infrastructure would have been affected, but Nloga insisted that flood risk had long been in the planning.

"The prime minister held an interdepartmental meeting during which he established a task force to ensure that the necessary arrangements and follow-up measures are put in place to safeguard both the competition venues and the accommodation sites."

With Formula 1 confirming its return to Africa earlier in October, global sport is slowly becoming a more regular event in Africa. As a result though, there have been questions asked about the legacy of such events.

Many in Senegal concerned by the high cost of living and unemployment will see these Games as an unnecessary expense. For the Senegalese authorities though, they are an opportunity for long-term investment in the country's young people as well as infrastructure. There is also the hope that this will make Dakar a major tourist destination.

There was further criticism of the Games being in Senegal from Human Rights Watch (HRW), with the NGO calling on the Senegalese authorities to change their stance on the LGBTQ+ community.

"You are welcoming all of the world. It shouldn't be 'you are welcome to our country, except this, except that,'" Larissa Kojoue from HRW told DW.

"Anti-LGBT legislation and that crackdown that is going on, they contradict the Olympic movement, the Olympic Charter, and also various human rights convention that the country has signed."

Earlier this year, Senegal President Bassirou Diomaye Faye signed into law new legislation on same-sex relations that have proved contentious abroad despite broad political support within the majority Muslim country's parliament. Several human rights groups had voiced concerns about the bill, including warning that it would dissuade people at risk of illnesses like HIV/AIDS from seeking help.

The Games were set to see the return of Russians to Olympic competition under their own colours after the International Olympic Committee (IOC) lifted their suspension in July.

However, the Russian Athletics Federation (RusAF) released a statement the day before the opening ceremony saying the reported 13 athletes (and 10 coaches) had been exluded from the competition. They demanded an explanation and asked for the decision to be reconsidered.

"The IOC-endorsed position was clear in its direction: young athletes holding Russian or Belarusian passports should no longer be restricted from international youth competitions. That principle should apply to Dakar 2026," read the statement.

Despite the IOC's ruling, each federation can still decide whether to authorize Russian participation. World Athletics, has clearly upheld their ban, while swimming and judo have allowed Russian athletes back.

"This has enabled World Athletics to pursue its own exclusory agenda in the face of clear and just directions from the IOC. This activism is only detrimental to youth sports, with the result being that Russian young athletes will be denied the opportunity to compete at these Games."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Despite the various concerns, there is an overriding hope that the Games will be prove beneficial for all involved.

"What makes the Youth Olympic Games in Dakar special is that they are also rooted in Senegal's extremely strong sporting culture," Nloga said.

"Every evening, when you take a stroll along the Corniche in Dakar, you're struck by the number of people you see exercising, regardless of their age or physical condition. What we'll be offering during these Olympic Games is also an immersion into Senegalese life – into the way sports are just as much a part of Senegalese identity."

This article was updated on October 30, 2026 to reflect the change in situation for Russian athletes at the Games.

#847. Thierno Barry double fires Everton to comeback win against Coventry

The wildly optimistic Evertonian – if such a being exists – could not have envisaged David Moyes’ side fifth in the Premier League with Thierno Barry just behind Erling Haaland in the goalscoring chart when their transfer window closed in calamitous fashion. Yet there they sit, team and striker defying all expectations, following a stirring comeback against luckless Coventry.

Frank Lampard endured a torturous night against his old club as Coventry impressed but were refused two strong penalty claims. The Coventry manager felt his team were denied a third time by the video assistant referee for an apparent handball by Barry when edging Everton ahead. Replays were inconclusive. It was the dancing French forward’s second goal of the game and 10th in all competitions this season. He also delivered a fine assist for Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall as the in-form midfielder put his latest England disappointment behind him to seal victory in convincing style.

It was a landmark occasion for Moyes as he equalled the great Harry Catterick’s record of 592 games in charge of Everton. “Seeing my name alongside Harry Catterick’s is hugely humbling and I hope I can continue to add to that figure,” the Scot wrote in his programme notes. “What I really hope, though, is that I can bring trophies to the club like Harry Catterick did.” Equalling Catterick’s collection of two league titles and an FA Cup may be beyond Moyes, who is in the final year of his Everton contract and working in very different times, but what he is doing with the smallest squad in the Premier League ranks as an achievement itself.

The Everton manager said post-match: “It’s great if I can build expectations because that means we are doing well but at some point someone is going to say ‘Look at the size of their squad’ and you might have to calm down. It might catch up with us at some point but I have to say the boys are doing really well.”

Moyes’ team laboured until falling behind to Yann Gboho’s opener early in the second half. From that moment they roused themselves and showed the clinical touch and smart decision-making that eluded Coventry, but luck was also on their side.

James Tarkowski survived two penalty appeals in one go when leaping between Caleb Yirenkyi and Ethan Pinnock to clear a Coventry free-kick. The Everton captain appeared to pull the former’s hair and raise an arm towards the latter’s face. Neither the referee, Stuart Attwell, nor the VAR, Timothy Wood, considered the hair-pull had met this season’s higher threshold for excessive force. Last season Tarkowski would have been sent off.

Lampard said: “The rules are fine. It’s not a red card and I kind of get that, but the rule remains it’s a foul so I felt it was a foul.” Coventry were denied a second penalty claim when Taiwo Awoniyi went down under a challenge from Vitalii Mykolenko. “Taiwo is on the line of the box and it is a penalty,” said Lampard. “I thought it was a penalty by the time Myko’s knee was in the back of Taiwo’s knee.”

Coventry finally, deservedly, got a break when benefiting from some abysmal Everton defending to take the lead. The influential Jack Rudoni was involved with a pass into Gboho who, with the aid of a deflection off Tarkowski, easily held off Merlin Röhl, Harrison Armstrong and Jarrad Branthwaite before poking a shot past the unsighted Jordan Pickford.

Less than 10 minutes later, and to general astonishment, Lampard’s team were behind. Tyler Dibling had been quiet on his first league start of the season but was involved in the Everton equaliser with a dangerous cross from the right. Coventry failed to clear and when Mykolenko swept in a cross at the second attempt Barry, showing good strength to hold off Jay Dasilva, beat Carl Rushworth with an emphatic header.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

The French striker soon reached double figures for the campaign when bundling home Tyrique George’s delivery to the far post. Dasilva made a mess of his attempted clearance and headed the ball against Barry – his hand, possibly – before it spun past Rushworth and over the line.

There was no questioning the legitimacy of Barry’s next goal involvement. The confident striker split the Coventry defence with a superb pass into Dewsbury-Hall, who ended his disappointing day on a high by racing clear and beating Rushworth with a precise finish inside the keeper’s near post.

Moyes called Barry’s display “fabulous”. He expanded: “Haaland’s worried about him catching him now! I don’t see many young centre-forwards scoring loads of goals in the Premier League. He’s settled down a bit more now. His language, his understanding and his communication is much better as well. Obviously he’s working hard to get in those positions to score. I’m really pleased for him.”

#846. Championship roundup: Birmingham go top, Cardiff stun Burnley from 4-1 down

Jay Stansfield earns Birmingham 2-1 win against Swansea

Cardiff stage remarkable fightback to beat Burnley 5-4

Jay Stansfield grabbed a late winner to fire Birmingham top of the Championship with a 2-1 win against 10-man Swansea.

Stansfield struck three minutes from time after a Christoph Klarer own goal had cancelled out his first-half opener for Birmingham.

Ryan Allsop saved Ross Stewart’s early Swansea penalty after the referee felt Jenson Seelt had been shoved over by Alex Cochrane from the first corner of the match. The referee intervened again when he sent off Marko Stamenic for a high challenge on Ethan Laird in the 26th minute.

“It’s great to be at the summit with everything we’ve been through and the whole journey,” said the Birmingham manager Chris Davies said.

Cardiff came from 4-1 down to snatch a dramatic 5-4 win against Burnley in a second successive goal-fest in the Welsh capital.

Cardiff had seen a 3-0 lead wiped out by West Ham to drop two points in midweek, but it was their turn to come from behind here as Burnley’s miserable season continued.

The visitors who opened the scoring when a hopeful punt forward from Lucas Pires allowed forward Andreas Hountondji to go through on goal and slide the ball past Nathan Trott.

Burnley doubled their lead 10 minutes later after great work on the left from Jaydon Banel. The ball came to Marcus Edwards on the edge of the box and he fired through a sea of bodies to beat Trott.

The hosts pulled one back before the break when Rubin Colwill’s goalbound effort bounced off Ollie Tanner and in but Kristian Bielik restored Burnley’s two-goal advantage before Alex Robertson diverted Aaron Ramsey’s cross into his own net to make it 4-1.

Yousef Salech – who had come off the bench less than two minutes before – began the comeback when he slotted home in the 65th minute and Jack Moylan made it 4-3 from the penalty spot with 15 minutes to go.

Salech headed his second goal of the game to level the scores in the 82nd minute with Robertson curling in a 30-yard wonder goal to secure the most unlikely of wins four minutes in time added on.

The Burnley manager, Fabio Celestini, said: “I can understand if there is fragility at 1-0, but it cannot happen at 4-1. It’s very difficult to accept the situation. Normally you don’t need to score four or five times to win a game, but that’s the reality.”

“It’s a very memorable day,” said the Cardiff manager Brian Barry-Murphy. “From the moment we got the second goal, I felt as though we became a very dangerous team, and the players’ belief was very evident.”

Jack McGlynn and Ben Wilmot scored as Stoke hit back to beat Portsmouth 2-1 and maintain their impressive form.

Tyrese Shade put Portsmouth in front after six minutes with a lovely bending finish, but Stoke turned a tame first half around to make it five away wins in a row. McGlynn capitalised on goalkeeper Nicolas Schmid’s failure to hold on to a cross before Wilmot headed home a rebound.

“That is the first time we have won five on the bounce away from home since 1947,” said the Stoke manager, Mark Robins. “That just shows what an achievement it is. The players need to take stock of that and be proud of it. We can go into the international break satisfied and it gives us a lot to be proud of going forward.

A magnificent display by Watford goalkeeper Federico Ravaglia denied Middlesbrough top spot as they were held to a 0-0 draw at Vicarage Road.

Middlesbrough drew a blank for the second time in four days as they rued the absence of top scorer Will Lankshear with a hamstring injury while under-pressure Watford head coach Alessio Dionisi had Ravaglia to thank for a third consecutive clean sheet at home.

Middlesbrough head coach Kim Hellberg said: “I’m very angry and disappointed because with all those chances created, all those beautiful attacks we had, it’s disappointing we didn’t win the game.”

Scott Parker is still waiting for his first win as West Ham manager after a 2-1 defeat at spirited Blackburn.

West Ham dominated possession but ultimately paid for profligacy early in the second half. Andri Gudjohnsen headed in his 10th league goal of the season and Dapo Afolayan’s powerful strike doubled the Rovers advantage 19 minutes from the end.

Joel Piroe lashed in from close range to halve the deficit and Tomas Soucek missed a glorious injury time chance as West Ham suffered their first away defeat of the campaign.

Parker said: “We’re bitterly disappointed because the result hasn’t gone our way. There are certain things that were big improvements. I’ve had one training session, 45 minutes yesterday. I see a committed group at this moment in time. A lot of work to be done but I’m looking forward to it.”

Second-half goals from Isaac Price, Jayson Molumby and substitute Felix Horn Myhre gave West Brom a 3-0 win against Millwall at The Hawthorns.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Price broke the deadlock with a superb, curling effort six minutes after the break before setting up Myhre for the 89th-minute third goal, after Molumby scored 12 minutes from time. A deserved return to winning ways made it six matches unbeaten for James Morrison’s side, who have now taken 13 points from their last 18.

James Morrison, the West Brom head coach, said: “One of our strengths is the energy and running power and we just outran them and played some nice football. The subs made a big impact which was important in a three-game week.”

Lewis O’Brien’s first goal of the season earned Wrexham a 1-1 draw and prevented Wolves going top. Wolves have never won at Cae Ras but Adam Armstrong’s strike after 25 minutes suggested they might register a history-making victory. Instead, O’Brien equalised for Phil Parkinson’s side two minutes later though the visitors still extended their unbeaten run to six matches.

Wrexham co-owners Ryan Reynolds and Rob McElhenney were in attendance for only this seventh league meeting between the sides in 102 years and first since 1988. Parkinson said: “It’s always very uplifting for the people who work at the club, the staff and the players when Rob and Ryan come over. The crowd too is uplifted with the owners being in town.”

Bristol City fans turned on Michael Skubala as Norwich made it nine goals in successive away victories with a 5-0 win at Ashton Gate. Norwich took a 22nd-minute lead when Paris Maghoma picked up the ball 40 yards out and ran forward unchallenged before placing a low shot past Brad Collins from the left side of the box.

It was 2-0 in the 53rd minute, Jason Knight’s mistimed header inside his own penalty area directing the ball to Harry Darling who coolly nodded it over Collins’ despairing dive. Three minutes later Maghoma turned provider, pulling a low cross back for Andre Brooks to fire home a third. There were still 20 minutes left when substitute Jovon Makama turned in an Anthony Musaba cross.

Mathias Kvistgaarden added the fifth with an 80th-minute penalty after being pulled down by Lisav Eissat as home fans chanted ‘You’re getting sacked in the morning’ in the direction of Skubala, whose team have already suffered five home league defeats this season.

Philippe Clement, the Norwich manager, said: “We are growing by the week. I am seeing boys becoming men, with clear signs of evolution from so many of our young players. That’s what we need if we are to get to where we want to be. The players are hungry and full of desire.”

Glen Kamara’s late goal gave QPR a 2-1 win over Lincoln City at Loftus Road. Richard Kone’s 11th-minute header – his fifth goal in four matches – put the hosts ahead before Dom Jefferies’ equaliser. Rangers endured a largely frustrating second half, but their persistence was rewarded in the 80th minute when Kamara thumped in his first goal since joining the club on a season-long loan from Rennes during the summer.

Julien Stephan, the QPR manager, said: “The players want to progress, they want to learn, and this was a good win for us. It doesn’t mean it was perfect – we can develop some things, especially in the last third to be more clinical – but I enjoyed it a lot.”

Jordan Thompson’s stunning volley secured Graham Alexander’s first win as Preston manager as his team shocked Southampton 1-0 at Deepdale.

Thompson won the match with a ferocious strike from outside the box in the 33rd minute and Preston held out for a vital three points.

Alexander said: “I’m chuffed for the players. I think they deserved it. I know it’s not always apparent but they have worked hard. They’re trying to believe in what we’re trying to do but they need that validation of performances and results to get that confidence and I think today will give us that.”

Substitute Matty Godden’s 79th-minute goal ended Charlton’s run of 11 league matches without victory as they defeated Sheffield United 2-1 at The Valley.

Millenic Alli’s first goal since his summer transfer from Luton put the hosts in front, but veteran Jordan Ayew levelled before the half-hour mark. Godden had only been on the pitch four minutes when he showed predatory instincts to hook in Alli’s cross at the near post and earn Charlton their first win since late August.

“Relief is a big thing – emotionally – because of everything that has gone on,” said the Charlton manager, Nathan Jones. “I’m really proud of the group, because they’ve had to cope with so much noise and pressure. It’s only one win, but it’s an important one.”

On Friday night, Derby’s manager, John Eustace, handed all the praise to his group of players after they came from behind to earn their first home victory of the season with a 3-1 win against Bolton.

Derby were heading for a third straight defeat when Rúben Rodrigues notched his second goal of the season to give the Bolton a half-time lead. The home fans booed the players off and then back on to the field after the break, which clearly had an effect when Ryan Nyambe equalised with his first goal in more than 300 career appearances just 39 seconds after the break. Jack Robinson put the hosts in front three minutes later before Rhian Brewster sealed a first win since September with his first of the season in stoppage time.

Eustace says a half-time team talk between the players helped shift the tide in the second period. He said: “It’s not about me, it’s about the group of players and I’m so pleased for them. The players have worked their socks off without any reward and then last two games we let ourselves down … Things haven’t been ideal but the way the group spoke was very pleasing for me.”

#844. NWSL playoffs: Cooper’s extra-time penalty sends Kansas City through as Utah stun San Diego

Michelle Cooper strikes in extra time to lift Current

Kansas City extend unbeaten home record with 1-0 win

Seventh-seeded Utah Royals upset San Diego Wave

Michelle Cooper converted an extra-time penalty to give the Kansas City Current a 1-0 victory over Angel City on Sunday in the quarter-finals of the National Women’s Soccer League playoffs.

The fourth-seeded Current will face the winner of Sunday’s quarter-final between top-seeded Gotham FC and No 8 Seattle Reign FC in next weekend’s semi-finals.

Kansas City, the only NWSL team to finish the regular season unbeaten at home, extended that run into the postseason.

Angel City goalkeeper Angelina Anderson made five saves in regulation. Four minutes into extra time, Kansas City defender Izzy Rodriguez sent in a corner kick. Before the ball went over the crossbar, Current defender Kayla Sharples went to ground near the goal line after contact with Anderson and midfielder Ary Borges. Kansas City were awarded a penalty, which Cooper converted.

The teams combined for 25 fouls in a physical encounter. Fifth-seeded Angel City collected three yellow cards in regulation, the first in the 13th minute when Sveindís Jónsdóttir slid into Gabrielle Robinson from behind as the Kansas City defender shielded the ball near her end line.

Borges was booked in the 58th minute after catching Vanessa DiBernardo with her cleat as they challenged for a ball in the air. In second-half stoppage time, Maiara Niehues clipped Cooper’s heel and knocked off her cleat. Kansas City’s only yellow card went to Temwa Chawinga in the 114th minute.

The seventh-seeded Utah Royals earned their first playoff victory with a 1-0 upset of the second-seeded San Diego Wave in Friday night’s NWSL quarter-final.

Cloé Lacasse delivered a pinpoint low cross to Kiana Palacios, who took a touch before firing home the game’s only goal in the 30th minute. It marked the first time Utah had led San Diego in any competition this season.

Royals goalkeeper Mandy McGlynn made four saves to record her sixth clean sheet of the season.

“Unbelievable, it’s just everything you could hope for,” McGlynn said. “I’m like in shock, no words can describe this feeling.”

The Royals snapped a four-match winless streak and will travel to face either the third-seeded Washington Spirit or sixth-seeded Portland Thorns in the semi-finals. Washington host Portland in Sunday’s remaining quarter-final.

Both teams were missing key players. San Diego midfielder Kimmi Ascanio was unavailable with a thigh injury, while Utah midfielder Mina Tanaka, initially listed as questionable with a hamstring injury, was ruled out.

The Wave were held scoreless despite dominating possession (62% to 38%), shots (16-8) and shots on target (5-2).

San Diego entered the match on a seven-match unbeaten run but have now lost four consecutive playoff matches.
